newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX PV electricity ends lower as cash eases.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX PV electricity ends lower as cash eases.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures ended mostly lower Wednesday with September Palo Verde (PV) falling off through the day in line with some easing in physical power prices, industry sources said.

September PV closed down 29 cents at $30.87 after trade in a range of $30.60-31.90 per megawatt hour (MWh) while October ended up three cents at $23.00 following exchanges in a range of $22.65-23.00 per MWh.
Remaining PV deferreds finished steady to two cents higher.
"Daily prices went through the roof, and when they just couldn't break through the new highs (in futures) everbody decided to get out of their length," one futures trader said.

September California Oregon Border (COB) settled down 96 cents at $23.29 after trades in a range of $23.25-25.00, while October closed down 18 cents at $22.02 following exchanges in a range of $21.90-22.20 per MWh.
Remaining COB deferreds finished between 10 cents higher and 30 cents lower.
NYMEX said an estimated total of 323 COB and 548 PV contracts traded.

Surging daily physical power prices in the West, which were said to be giving futures strength early in the day, were reported to have backed off highs in the afternoon with expectations hot weather was turning milder.
Next-day peak PV was talked at near $100.00 per MWh Wednesday afternoon from an early afternoon reported high of $175.00 per MWh.

Much above normal temperatures in Arizona, Nevada, southern Utah and California were expected to cool to three to six degrees above normal by the weekend. Colorado and New Mexico, where cool weather was expected today, was called to moderate to slightly below normal levels over the weekend.
In the Pacific Northwest, temperatures were forecast to cool to near-normal levels Friday and Saturday.
Forecasts for August 10-14 called for near-normal temperatures through much of the West, with the exception of Oregon and Washington state, which were expected to see above-normal temperatures.

Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP) said Wednesday it projected another record in peak electricity demand on its system due to sizzling summer heat over its service territory for a second day.
On Tuesday, soaring energy usage for cooling pushed peak demand on LADWP's system to a record at 5,336 megawatts (MW).

In generation news, a 750 MW unit at the Ormond Beach power plant in Ventura County, Calif., which tripped off line Tuesday due to a voltage dip caused by the line outage, was returned to operation, a spokesman said.

SoCal Edison said Wednesday the voltage dip was caused when two 500 kilovolt (kv) high-voltage transmission lines near Los Angeles were knocked out of service when a light plane crashed into them Tuesday. The lines had been restored to service Wednesday.
Also, two 700 MW coal-fired power generators that tripped off line Tuesday at the Colstrip power complex in Montana were said to be back in service Wednesday.
Electricity output from the 1,221 MW Palo Verde nuclear power unit 3 in Wintersburg, Ariz., held at 90 percent power early Wednesday for repairs to a condensate pump.
The adjacent 1,221 MW Palo Verde nuclear power unit 2 was operating at 91 percent of capacity as of early Wednesday as the unit coasts down to a scheduled refueling outage September 6.
Water flow into regional hydroelectric systems in the Northwest and Canada has been slowed in recent days to refill reservoirs for fish migration requirements.
Separately, the operating limit on the Pacific Intertie transmission system was to have been increased to 6,900 MW from 6,300 MW as of 2400 PDT Tuesday.
The 6,900 MW limit will continue until the next seasonal operating plan is put together and reviewed by the Western System Coordinating Council.
((--Chris Reese, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1627))
